source_text: αὐτά, τούτων καὶ ἡ οὐσία μία καθέστηκεν· ἵν' ἀκολουθῇ τὸ ὑπὸ ὁμοίου ὅμοιον χαρακτηρίζεσθαι. 11.7 τῷ γὰρ ἀληθινῷ καὶ ἀϊδίῳ φωτί, πρὸς τὸ ἀληθινὸν καὶ ἀΐδιον φῶς, καὶ τῇ ὄντως .......... 15.1 «ἐγὼ ὁ θεός, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλος πλὴν ἐμοῦ. δίκαιος καὶ σωτὴρ οὐκ ἔστιν πάρεξ ἐμοῦ. ἐπιστράφητε πρός με καὶ σωθήσεσθε, οἱ ἀπ' ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς. ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ θεός, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλος. κατ' ἐμαυτοῦ ὀμνύω· ἦ μὴν ἐξελεύ σεται ἐκ τοῦ στόματός μου δικαιοσύνη καὶ οἱ λόγοι μου οὐκ ἀποστραφήσον ται, ὅτι ἐμοὶ κάμψει πᾶν γόνυ καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ὀμιεῖται τὸν θεόν», ὅ ἐστιν ἐπιγνώσεται τὸν θεὸν ἤ «ἐξομολογήσεται τῷ θεῷ». 15.2 οὐκ ἔστιν οὖν ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ υἱοῦ ὁ θεὸς καὶ πατήρ, οὐ τῷ ἀνάρχῳ, οὐ τῇ οὐσίᾳ, οὐ τῇ δόξῃ, ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἴσης, πλὴν εἰ μή που τῷ τῆς πατρότητος λόγῳ. 15.3 ὅτι γὰρ τοῦ μονογενοῦς υἱοῦ τὰ ῥήματα, ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος Ῥωμαίοις γράφων ἐσαφήνισεν οὕτως εἰπών· «πάντες γὰρ παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ καθὼς γέγραπται· «ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος, ὅτι ἐμοὶ κάμψει πᾶν γόνυ καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολο γήσεται τῷ θεῷ»». 15.4 Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ θεολόγος Ἰωάννης ἐν μὲν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ εἶπεν· 15.4 «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν. πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἓν ὁ γέγονεν. ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλα βεν». 15.5 ἐν δὲ τῇ Ἀποκαλύψει· «ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν ὁ παντοκράτωρ». 15.6 Τό «ὁ ὤν» σημαίνει τὸ ἀεὶ ὂν τῆς θείας ὑποστάσεως καθὰ καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ ἔφαμεν. ἀόριστος γὰρ ἡ λέξις, ὅθεν ὄνομα ἑαυτοῦ ὁ θεὸς εἶπεν τό «ὁ ὤν». 15.7 Τό «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν» ποιεῖ προῦπτον καὶ σφόδρα γε συμφανὲς τὸ ἄτοπον καὶ φευκτὸν τοῦ «ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν». ἡ γὰρ λέξις ἡ «ἦν» ἀπαρέμφατός ἐστιν. ῥωμαϊστὶ δὲ ἡ ἀπαρέμφατος ἐκ δύο λέξεων σύγκειται· πλῃσθῃαμπερφεξτῃς, ἑρμηνεύεται δέ· πλέον ἢ τέλειος. 15.8 ὥστε νῦν ἀπαιτεῖ νοηθῆναι ὑπεράχρονος ἢ ἄναρχος. τὸ γὰρ οὐκ ὢν ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ εἴ τις ἂν εἴποι, ἀρχή ποτε ἀναίτιος οὐκ ἦν. καὶ πάλιν, ὁ μηδέπω ὢν χρόνος τοῦ ποιήσαντος αὐτὸν πῶς εἶναι μέτρον δύναται; 15.9 Τό «ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν» παριστᾷ, ἣν υἱὸς ἔχει πρὸς θεὸν πατέρα φύσεως οἰκειότητα, καὶ 7 τό–ἀφ' οὗ ἦν, εἰ θέμις οὕτως εἰπεῖν, ὁ αὐτογενὴς πατήρ–συνυπάρχειν αὐτῷ τὸν ἐξ αὐτοῦ υἱόν. 15.10 ἐρρωμένως δὲ νοηθείη ἂν τό «ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν», ὅτι κατὰ τὸν θεὸν ἦν ἄναρχος, ἀγένητος, ἀχώρητος, ἀγαθός, ἀθάνατος, παμβασιλεύς. εἰ γὰρ μὴ οὕτως ἔχει ἐπὶ τῆς βρυθείσης σοφίας ταύτης, οὐχ ἕξει οὐδ' ἐπὶ τῆς πηγῆς τῆς βρυσάσης τὴν σοφίαν. ἔχει δὲ οὕτως ἐπ' ἀμφοῖν. 15.11 ἐπιφανὴς γὰρ καὶ βέβαιος καὶ ἀπερίεργος καὶ πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ὁρῶν μόνον ὁ σκοπὸς καὶ ὁ θεοπαράδοτος λόγος τοῦ Ἰωάννου. 15.12 Τό «θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος» συνιστᾷ τὸ οὐσιώδη εἶναι τὸν λόγον καὶ θεὸν εἶναι οἷός ἐστιν θεὸς ἐκεῖνος οὗ λόγος ἐστίν· καὶ αὖθις τὸ ἀναίτιον. 15.13 Τό «πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἕν» ἀποφαίνει αὐτόν, ὡς ἤδη ἐλέχθη, μονονουχὶ δημιουργόν, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ οὐκ ἐκτίσθη. 15.14 εἰ γὰρ μηδὲ ἓν κτιστὸν χωρὶς αὐτοῦ τὸ εἶναι ἐδέξατο, παντί που δῆλον ὡς αὐτὸς οὐκ ἐγένετο, ἀλλ' ἐγεννήθη θεϊκῶς. καὶ γὰρ ἀμήχανον ἐκ μὴ ὄντων εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἥκειν τὸν ὕπαρξιν τοῖς ὅλοις καὶ τοῖς λογικοῖς οὐσίωσιν καὶ ἀθανασίαν δεδωκότα. οὐδὲν γὰρ κτιστὸν οὐσιοῦν ἢ ἀπαθανατοῦν ἢ λογικοὺς ποιεῖν δύναται· ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς ἤδη παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων παραχθείσης οὐσίας χρυσοῦ ἢ ἀργύρου ἢ χαλκοῦ ἢ σιδήρου ἢ ξύλου ἢ λίθου δημιουργοῖ ἄψυχον καὶ ἄλογον, ἀνδριάντα τυχὸν ἤ τι ἕτερον· 15.15 αὐτὸ δέ, οὐσίαν μὴ οὖσαν προοῖσαι ἢ ἔμψυχον καὶ λογικὴν ἀναδεῖξαι μόνης τῆς πανδυνάμου καὶ αὐτοτελοῦς μιᾶς θεϊκῆς φύσεως ἴδιον καὶ ἐξαίρετον τυγχάνει ὄν. 15.16 ἐποίησεν δὲ δι' αὐτοῦ ὁ πατὴρ ὡς φῶς δι' οἰκείου ἀπαυγάσματος καὶ ὡς νοῦς διὰ λόγου. 15.17 Τό «ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν» ἐπεκδιδάσκει ὅτι αὐτός ἐστιν ἀνάρχως, ἡ ζωὴ τῆς μιᾶς καὶ ἀνωτάτω φύσεως ὑπάρχων, καὶ μηδαμῶς ὄντων πάντων αἴτιος ὢν τῶν ὄντων. διὸ καὶ αὐτός φησιν· «ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωή, ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς». 15.18 φιλοτιμεῖται δὲ τῷ ἀνάρχῳ τὰς μαρτυρίας τοσαυτάκις εἰπὼν τό «ἦν», ἵνα τῇ συνεχείᾳ τῆς τοιαύτης φωνῆς ἢ αἱρετικῶν τὰς κωφὰς ἀκοὰς διανοίξῃ ἢ μηδὲν περὶ τοῦ «ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν» ἐν τῇ μελλούσῃ καθολικῇ καὶ ἀπαρεγκλίτῳ διαγνώσει πρόφασις ὑπολειφθείη. 15.19 Τό «καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων» ἐκπαιδεύει αὖθις τὰ αὐτά. φησὶν γάρ· αὕτη ἡ
pass_a_gloss: [...the] same, of these the essence too stands one; so that it follows that like is characterized by like. 11.7 For to the true and eternal light, in relation to the true and eternal light, and to the truly [the copy-text breaks off with dots; the text resumes at 15.1] 15.1 'I [am] God, and there is no other besides me. Righteous and saviour there is not except me. Turn toward me and you will be saved, those from the end of the earth. I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear: truly righteousness will go out from my mouth and my words will not be turned back, that to me every knee will bend and every tongue will swear by God', which is, will recognize God, or 'will confess to God'. 15.2 So God and Father is not before the Son, not in the beginningless, not in the essence, not in the glory, but on equal footing, except perhaps in the account of the fatherhood. 15.3 For that the words are of the only-begotten Son, the divine Paul writing to Romans made clear, saying thus: 'for we will all stand beside the judgment seat of Christ, as it has been written: I live, says the Lord, that to me every knee will bend and every tongue will confess to God'. 15.4 And likewise the theologian John also, in the Gospel, said: 15.4 'in beginning was the Word, and the Word was toward God, and God was the Word. This one was in beginning toward God. All things came to be through him, and without him came to be not even one thing which has come to be. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not seize it'. 15.5 And in the Revelation: 'the one being and the one who was and the one coming, Lord our God the ruler of all'. 15.6 The 'the one being' signifies the everlasting being of the divine hypostasis, just as we said elsewhere too. For the expression is unbounded, whence God said 'the one being' as name of himself. 15.7 The 'in beginning was' makes visible beforehand and indeed very clear the absurd thing, to be shunned, of 'there was when he was not'. For the word 'was' is indefinite. And in the Roman tongue the indefinite is composed of two words, the [Latin] pluperfect, and it is interpreted: more than perfect. 15.8 So that now it demands [him] to be understood as beyond timelessness or without beginning. For if someone should say the 'not being in the beginning', a causeless beginning once was not. And again, time which was not yet, how can it be measure of the one who made it? 15.9 The 'was toward God' presents the belonging of nature which a Son has toward God the Father, and that, since when the self-originate Father was, if it is right to say so, the Son from him coexists with him. 15.10 And the 'was toward God' might be understood strongly, that like God he was without beginning, unoriginate, uncontainable, good, immortal, king of all. For if it is not so in the case of this wisdom that welled out, it will not be so either in the case of the spring that welled out the wisdom. But it is so in the case of both. 15.11 For manifest and firm and free of idle curiosity and looking toward the divine alone is the aim and the word handed down from God of John. 15.12 The 'God was the Word' establishes the Word being substantial and being God such as that God is whose Word he is; and again the causeless. 15.13 The 'all things came to be through him, and without him came to be not even one' shows him, as already was said, not only craftsman, but that he also was not created. 15.14 For if not even one created thing received being without him, it is surely plain to all that he himself did not come to be, but was begotten in godlike manner. And indeed it is impossible that the one who has given existence to the wholes and to the rational ones the giving of essence and immortality came from things not being into being. For nothing created can give essence or make immortal or make rational ones; but from the substance of gold or silver or bronze or iron or wood or stone already brought forth by God from things not being, it would craft a soulless and reasonless thing, a statue perhaps or something else; 15.15 but this itself, to bring forth an essence not being or to show it ensouled and rational, happens to be the own and select [property] of the sole all-powerful and self-complete one divine nature. 15.16 And the Father made through him as light through its own radiance and as mind through word. 15.17 The 'in him was life' teaches further that he is beginninglessly, being the life of the one and highest nature, and, all things in no way being, being cause of the things that are. pass_b_english: … same, their essence too stands as one, so that it follows that like is marked out by like. For to the true and eternal light, in relation to the true and eternal light, and to the truly [...]

“I am God, and there is no other besides me. There is no righteous one and Saviour except me. Turn to me and you will be saved, you who are from the end of the earth. I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear: righteousness shall surely go out of my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back, that to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear by God” (Isaiah 45:21-23), which means, will acknowledge God, or “will confess to God.”

So God the Father is not ahead of the Son, not in being without beginning, not in essence, not in glory. They stand on equal terms, except perhaps in the matter of fatherhood. For that these are the words of the only-begotten Son the inspired Paul made clear when he wrote to the Romans, saying: “For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, as it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God” (Romans 14:10-11).

Likewise John the theologian too said in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it” (John 1:1-5). And in the Revelation: “He who is and who was and who is to come, the Lord our God, the Almighty” (Revelation 1:8).

“He who is” signifies the everlasting being of the divine hypostasis, as we have said elsewhere too. For the expression is without limit, and that is why God gave “He who is” as his own name (Exodus 3:14).

“In the beginning was” (John 1:1) sets in plain view, and makes very clear indeed, how absurd and how much to be shunned is the saying “There was when he was not.” For the word “was” is indefinite. In Latin this indefinite form is made up of two words, the “pluperfect,” which is rendered “more than perfect.” So here it requires that he be understood as beyond time altogether, or without beginning. For if anyone were to say that he was not in the beginning, then the beginning, which has no cause, would once not have been. And again, how can time, which did not yet exist, be the measure of the one who made it?

“Was with God” (John 1:1) sets before us the kinship of nature that the Son has with God the Father, and that from the time the self-originate Father was (if it is lawful to say so) the Son who is from him exists together with him. “Was with God” could also be understood in a strong sense: that like God he was without beginning, unoriginate, uncontainable, good, immortal, King of all. For if this were not so with the wisdom that has welled up, it would not be so with the spring that sent the wisdom welling up either. But it is so with both. For John’s aim, and his word handed down from God, is clear, firm, free of idle subtlety, and looks to the divine alone.
“The Word was God” (John 1:1) establishes that the Word has real being, and that he is God such as that God is whose Word he is; and again, that he has no cause.

“All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being” (John 1:3) shows him, as has been said already, to be not only Creator, but also not created. For if not one created thing received its being without him, it is plain to everyone that he himself did not come into being, but was begotten as God is begotten. Indeed, it is impossible that he who gave existence to the universe, and essence and immortality to rational beings, should have come from non-being into being. For nothing created can give essence, or immortality, or make beings rational. It works only on the substance of gold, or silver, or bronze, or iron, or wood, or stone, already brought out of non-being by God, and from it fashions something without soul or reason, a statue perhaps, or something else. But this very thing, to bring forth an essence that was not, or to show it forth as living and rational, is the peculiar and singular property of the one all-powerful and self-complete divine nature alone. And the Father made all things through him as light makes through its own radiance, and as mind through word.

“In him was life” (John 1:4) teaches us further that he is without beginning, being the life of the one supreme nature, and that when nothing at all existed he was the cause of the things that exist. That is why he himself says, “I am the life” (John 14:6), “I am the light” (John 8:12).

He is lavish with testimonies to the one without beginning, saying “was” so many times, so that by repeating such a word he might either open the deaf ears of heretics, or leave no pretext at all for “There was when he was not” at the coming universal and unswerving judgment.
“And the life was the light of men” (John 1:4) teaches the same things once more. For he says: this …

choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English split 15.9 across two paragraphs and garbled it ('presents that which has a Son. Regarding God the Father, the indwelling of nature'); turned ὅτι … τοῦ μονογενοῦς υἱοῦ τὰ ῥήματα (15.3, that the words are the Son's) into 'regarding the words'; ἀπερίεργος into 'unsearchable'; οὐσιώδη into 'of the essence'; garbled 15.14 ('for existence to reach from non-being to being through those things which have been granted essence ... by the whole and the rational'); turned the genitive absolute μηδαμῶς ὄντων πάντων (15.17, when nothing existed) into 'in no way being the cause'; and used bracket fillers ([missing], [pre-existence], [unintelligible], [is]). References: Isaiah 45:22 and 45:23 replaced by Isaiah 45:21-23 for the whole quotation; Romans 14:11 widened to 14:10-11; 'Isa', 'Rom', 'Rev' written in full; 'I am the light' given John 8:12 (the old draft hung John 14:6 on both sayings); Exodus 3:14 and each John 1 lemma cited.

choices.term: αὐτά, τούτων καὶ ἡ οὐσία μία
choices.english: … same, their essence too stands as one
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence, finishing 11.6 ('those whose names are the same'); only the words this section holds are translated, with a leading ellipsis.
Bracketed lacuna: the copy-text breaks off with dots in 11.7 and resumes at 15.1; nothing is supplied.

choices.term: ὅ ἐστιν ἐπιγνώσεται τὸν θεὸν ἢ «ἐξομολογήσεται τῷ θεῷ»
choices.english: which means, will acknowledge God, or “will confess to God.”
choices.why: Didymus explains 'swear by God' and gives the wording Paul uses in Romans 14:11; the explanation is his, not Isaiah's.
A garbled Greek transliteration of the Latin grammatical term plusquamperfectus, which Didymus glosses 'more than perfect'. Given by its English name so the reader can follow; see problems.
Rare compound ('above the timeless'); rendered so it reads aloud without inventing a claim.

choices.term: ἀφ' οὗ ἦν … ὁ αὐτογενὴς πατήρ
choices.english: from the time the self-originate Father was
choices.why: ἀφ' οὗ is temporal: the Son coexists with the Father from the moment the Father is, i.e. always. Didymus' hedge εἰ θέμις οὕτως εἰπεῖν is kept.
κατά with the accusative of likeness; the old 'according to God' hid the sense.

choices.english: the wisdom that has welled up … the spring that sent the wisdom welling up
choices.why: Keeps Didymus' spring image for Son and Father.

choices.term: μονονουχὶ δημιουργόν, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ οὐκ ἐκτίσθη
choices.english: to be not only Creator, but also not created
choices.why: μονονουχί normally means 'all but'; with the following ἀλλ' ὅτι καί it must stand for μόνον οὐχί, 'not only'. See problems.
Adverb 'in a godlike manner': the begetting befits God, unlike coming into being.

choices.term: φιλοτιμεῖται δὲ τῷ ἀνάρχῳ τὰς μαρτυρίας
choices.english: He is lavish with testimonies to the one without beginning
choices.why: The subject is John, who repeats 'was'; the dative names the one the testimonies honour.

choices.term: ἐξελεύ σεται, ἀποστραφήσον ται, κατέλα βεν, ἐξομολο γήσεται
choices.why: Words split by line breaks in the copy-text; read as single words.
The '7' is a printed line number in the copy-text (page debris); skipped. The edition numbers 15.4 printed twice are anchors only.
